key_finding: Across six agents on BrowseComp-Plus and BrowseComp, answer accuracy correlates with cumulative retrieval recall far more than with number of searches or context consumed, and top agents issue fewer redundant queries despite useful evidence often appearing early.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis using human-annotated document-level relevance judgments, decomposing failures into retrieval gaps vs utilization gaps, retrieval model and harness held fixed across six agents.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the assumption that more search effort drives agentic gains: it shows the gain tracks evidence quality, not search volume, which reframes what our C2 mechanism analysis should measure (stopping criteria and evidence selection, not query count).
limitations: evaluated on two benchmarks only (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp)
diagnostic study, not a new system or benchmark
relevance_reason: A trajectory-level diagnosis that separates retrieval from utilization failure and shows search effort is only weakly tied to quality, exactly the kind of gain-scrutiny the brief's question 4 asks for.

key_finding: PaSa-7B, an RL-trained autonomous paper-search agent, beats the best Google+GPT-4o baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on a real-world academic query benchmark.
methodology: RL-trained LLM agent that issues searches, reads papers, and selects references; trained on synthetic AutoScholarQuery (35k queries) and evaluated on a new real-world RealScholarQuery benchmark.
why_it_matters: Establishes the single-query search-engine baseline (Google, Google Scholar) this whole literature repeatedly measures against, and its two benchmarks are the construction template later papers critique or reuse.
limitations: trained on synthetic data with only limited real-world validation
benchmark scope is AI conference papers, not broader science
relevance_reason: One of the founding agentic-paper-search systems, defining both the recall-ceiling baseline (C1) and a widely cited benchmark construction (C4).

key_finding: A bounded pipeline of single seed search, 1.5-hop citation expansion, entailment-based edge pruning, and recency-aware random-walk ranking outperforms open-ended deep research agents by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost on LitSearch-style benchmarks.
methodology: Structured, inspectable graph-exploration system (Crase) evaluated on LitSearch and a second benchmark over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus, compared against deep research agents built on proprietary models.
why_it_matters: Directly isolates which agentic move (citation-graph traversal with explicit pruning) carries the gain over an undifferentiated agent loop, and shows a bounded design can beat open-ended search decisively cheaper.
limitations: only two benchmarks tested
relies on entailment model quality for edge pruning, itself unvalidated against ground truth
relevance_reason: Precisely answers the brief's question 2: attributes measured gains to a specific mechanism (bounded citation-graph traversal) rather than treating the agent as a black box.

key_finding: Across eight expert-conceived literature review tasks, overlap between human- and mid-2025 LLM-selected references was under 6%, and 64% of AI-generated references had at least one incorrect metadata field, though a later 2026 model showed zero fabrication or mismatch in a single-project test.
methodology: Controlled parallel study: human experts and AI systems (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini, later ChatGPT Pro 5.5) perform identical literature-review tasks on eight physics/astro/cosmology projects; overlap and hallucination rates measured.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that current agentic literature search already matches competent human search; puts a concrete ceiling (near-zero overlap, majority-hallucinated metadata) on what today's systems deliver before verification.
limitations: small sample of eight projects
domain-specific to physics/astro/cosmology
improvement claim for the 2026 model rests on a single project
relevance_reason: The strongest evidence in this set for the brief's premise-testing mandate: real human-benchmarked comparison showing current agentic literature search substantially underperforms expert search.

key_finding: WisPaper's agentic Deep Search module reaches 22.26% recall on TaxoBench versus 20.92% for an O3 baseline, with its validation model achieving 93.70% accuracy at flagging hallucinated candidates.
methodology: End-to-end agent system combining keyword retrieval with an LLM-based validation module (WisModel); evaluated on TaxoBench, abstract-only detail on benchmark construction.
why_it_matters: The margin over the single-query-style O3 baseline is small (~1.3 points), which is itself useful evidence against the premise that agentic search reliably delivers large recall gains.
limitations: TaxoBench construction not described
gain over baseline is marginal and not decomposed by mechanism
relevance_reason: A recent agentic scholar-search system reporting only a modest recall gain over a plain baseline, relevant to testing how large reported agentic gains really are.

key_finding: ReBOL combines LLM query reformulation with Bayesian-optimization-guided relevance scoring to beat LLM reranker baselines, e.g. 46.5% vs 35.0% recall@100 on Robust04 at comparable latency.
methodology: Bayesian optimization over a multimodal relevance posterior seeded by LLM query reformulations, iteratively updated via batched LLM relevance judgments; evaluated on five BEIR datasets with two LLMs.
why_it_matters: A concrete retrieval/reranking technique that could underlie the retrieval stage of a literature-search agent, showing reformulation alone is insufficient without a better top-k retrieval strategy — informs what 'agentic mechanism' claims should actually be compared against.
limitations: evaluated on general BEIR IR datasets, not scientific-literature-search benchmarks
no test in an actual multi-step literature-search agent
relevance_reason: Directly evaluates a retrieval/reranking method combining query reformulation with a smarter scoring loop, relevant to the mechanisms underlying agentic literature search even though tested on general IR data.

key_finding: Removing followable cross-reference links roughly doubles search cost per grounded fact as corpus scale grows to 5000 pages, but content deemed 'unreachable by search' could still be recovered via read-derived re-queries in the link-stripped condition.
methodology: Pre-registered two-arm controlled experiment on a deterministic generated wiki-style corpus (50/500/5000 pages) with and without real hyperlinks, measured via 99 episodes of a Claude agent using search/fetch tools.
why_it_matters: Shows a rigorous, controlled measurement design for isolating what link/graph traversal contributes to agent search cost and coverage — a template for cleanly separating 'citation-graph traversal' contribution from search alone, and a caution that 'unreachable' claims depend on query-generation strategy.
limitations: synthetic organizational wiki corpus, not a scientific literature corpus
document-completion task rather than literature search
relevance_reason: Rigorous controlled study of cross-reference/link traversal's contribution to agent search cost, analogous in design to citation-graph traversal questions, though set in a non-literature wiki corpus.

key_finding: LATTICE, an LLM-guided hierarchical search index with no embedding model at search time, matches the best fine-tuned ensemble on BRIGHT (46.7 nDCG@10) and reaches 49.1 with a lightweight ensemble, while remaining competitive on SciFact and SciDocs.
methodology: Top-down LLM-guided construction of a hierarchical search index from multi-level document summaries plus calibrated path-aggregated LLM traversal, evaluated on BRIGHT, NQ, SciFact, SciDocs.
why_it_matters: Shows that bypassing the embedding-retriever bottleneck entirely via LLM-guided hierarchical traversal can match or beat query-side reformulation fixes on reasoning-intensive retrieval, directly informing which retrieval architecture underlies a literature-search agent's evidence-gathering stage.
limitations: BRIGHT is a general reasoning-intensive benchmark, not literature-search specific
token-budget tradeoffs mean reranking still wins at low budgets
relevance_reason: A retrieval/reranking method explicitly targeting the standard embedding-retriever-then-verify recipe's failure mode, tested partly on scientific IR benchmarks (SciFact, SciDocs).

key_finding: On a fixed, human-verified corpus, Search-R1 with BM25 achieves only 3.86% accuracy while GPT-5 reaches 55.9%, and pairing GPT-5 with a stronger embedding retriever raises accuracy to 70.1% with fewer search calls.
methodology: New benchmark derived from BrowseComp using a fixed curated corpus with human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled disentanglement of retriever from agent.
why_it_matters: Sets the canonical fair baseline for comparing retriever choice against agentic reasoning improvements, and its corpus/labeling method is the construction standard against which other benchmarks in this space (and their contamination controls) should be judged.
limitations: corpus assembled per-query from supporting docs plus mined negatives, which later work shows may inflate ease relative to a realistic corpus
single benchmark family (BrowseComp derivative)
relevance_reason: The reference benchmark for disentangling retrieval-method contribution from agent design in deep research systems, directly answering the brief's baseline-ceiling and benchmark-construction questions.

key_finding: Deep research agents exhibit 'inertia bias' — reduced objectivity when judging outcomes of their own prior actions — measured via the new IBIS benchmark, and context-isolating this bias at two decision points (NIS-Agent) cuts token cost by 33% while maintaining competitive performance across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh.
methodology: Controlled benchmark (IBIS) holding search observations fixed while varying self-authorship of the prior action; NIS-Agent applies context isolation at webpage-triage and answer-validation steps, tested across four deep-research benchmarks plus an 8B fine-tuned model.
why_it_matters: Identifies a specific, previously unnamed failure mode that inflates or distorts self-reported agentic gains via biased self-judgment, meaning apparent 'agentic mechanism' improvements may partly reflect corrected judgment bias rather than better search — directly bears on how gains should be measured.
limitations: evaluated across general deep-research benchmarks, not literature-search-specific ones
IBIS is a new, narrowly-scoped diagnostic benchmark
relevance_reason: Surfaces a mechanism-level bias that confounds measured agentic gains, informing how the scan should interpret reported improvements and what to control for when comparing systems.

key_finding: HySemRAG's structured field extraction achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity than PDF-chunking approaches (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001), with 68.3% single-pass success and 99.0% citation accuracy in an agentic literature-synthesis pipeline.
methodology: Multi-stage ETL+RAG pipeline combining semantic search, keyword filtering, and knowledge-graph traversal with agentic self-correction and post-hoc citation verification; evaluated on 643 observations from 60 testing sessions, applied to geospatial epidemiology literature.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a hybrid retrieval-plus-graph-traversal architecture for literature synthesis with concrete citation-accuracy and extraction-quality numbers, useful as a retrieval/reranking design reference even though not benchmarked against a single-query baseline.
limitations: no comparison against a single-query search baseline
single-author preprint applied to an epidemiology case study rather than literature-search-agent benchmarks
evaluation set (643 observations, 60 sessions) not described as a standard benchmark
relevance_reason: A hybrid retrieval/knowledge-graph system for automated literature synthesis, directly on the C3 retrieval-method question, though weaker on baseline comparison and generality.

key_finding: A systematic taxonomy of Deep Research agents along information-acquisition strategy (API vs browser), tool-use modularity, and planning/composition architecture, paired with a critical evaluation identifying restricted external-knowledge access, sequential-execution inefficiency, and metric-objective misalignment as key current benchmark limitations.
methodology: Narrative systematic review and taxonomy construction over the Deep Research agent literature, with a maintained repository of surveyed systems.
why_it_matters: Names the exact benchmark-construction failure modes (restricted knowledge access, misaligned metrics) the brief's question 3 and 4 are asking about, giving a map of where existing evaluations are already known to be shaky.
limitations: narrative synthesis, not a systematic-protocol review
no new empirical results of its own
relevance_reason: The field's own synthesis of architecture types and benchmark weaknesses, providing the orientation and critique the brief's decisions 2 and 3 depend on.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus's evidence into a 553M-document corpus not built from benchmark queries drops the strongest agent's evidence recall from 84.3% to 21.4% (with a 63% increase in search calls) while answer accuracy falls by only five points, on 57 fully-verified projected questions.
methodology: Projection pipeline decomposing questions into atomic reasoning hops, grounding each hop in a new corpus (ClimbMix) built independent of the benchmark, retaining only questions verified by automatic checks, an independent agent, and human review.
why_it_matters: A direct demonstration that a benchmark's own construction (query-conditioned corpus and negatives) inflates measured retrieval performance; the same agent's evidence recall collapses on a corpus not assembled per-query, exactly the replication failure the brief's question 4 is looking for.
limitations: only 57 questions survive the strict grounding-verification pipeline
single projection target (ClimbMix); generality to other corpora untested
relevance_reason: The clearest evidence in this set that reported agentic-search gains can shrink dramatically once benchmark construction artifacts (query-conditioned corpora) are removed.

key_finding: PaperPilot-9B raises Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5 over the base toolset agent, while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: Trains a 9B multi-turn agent via supervised workflow imitation and preference optimization over DAG-structured search workflows (keyword search, citation expansion, filtering, scoring, reranking, evidence extraction); evaluated in a multi-turn interaction setting.
why_it_matters: Shows explicit, editable workflows—not undifferentiated agent reasoning—drive the measured gain over a toolset baseline, informing how we'd decompose which agentic move (reformulation vs citation expansion vs reranking) is doing the work.
limitations: gain is measured against a toolset agent baseline, not a single-query database search baseline
no ablation isolating which individual operator drives the improvement
relevance_reason: Directly proposes and evaluates a multi-turn scientific literature search agent combining query refinement, citation expansion, and reranking — core to decisions 1-2.

key_finding: EviReform's evidence-guided residual query reformulation for graph retrieval beats the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Introduces residual query formulation from retrieved passages, combined with normalized propagation over an entity-linked proposition graph; evaluated on three multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Isolates query reformulation as the specific mechanism carrying a graph-retrieval gain, giving a quantified move-level effect size to compare against literature-search agents that bundle reformulation and traversal together.
limitations: evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature search corpora
no single-query database search baseline reported
relevance_reason: A clean, quantified example of query-reformulation-attributed gain in graph retrieval — the mechanism decision 2 asks about, though tested outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: Across 26 full-text-coded AI-scientist systems, 83% release code but only 38% release execution traces/seeds and 38% report any novelty-verification method, and no closed-loop system demonstrates an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Survey screening 125 candidate works, full-text coding 26 systems across seven audit dimensions (lifecycle stage, autonomy, evaluation, artifacts, human-in-loop, novelty verification, result-selection disclosure).
why_it_matters: Documents a field-wide auditability gap in claim verification for autonomous research agents, bearing on how much we should trust self-reported agentic literature-search gains absent replication artifacts.
limitations: covers the full AI-scientist lifecycle, not literature search specifically
narrative/coded survey rather than direct benchmark evidence
relevance_reason: A survey of verification practices across autonomous research agents, relevant to how skeptically we weigh reported gains (decision 4) even though its scope is broader than literature search alone.

key_finding: PaSaMaster achieves 16.5x higher F1 than Google Scholar and 37.8% higher F1 than GPT-5.2 at about 1% of the cost, reducing source hallucination from 32.66% to zero across 38 disciplines in PaSaMaster-Bench.
methodology: Recursive self-evolving agentic retrieval system separating LLM-based intent understanding from lightweight-model retrieval/scoring over verified papers; evaluated on a custom 38-discipline benchmark against Google Scholar and GPT-5.2 baselines.
why_it_matters: Directly anchors the recall/precision ceiling of a single-query search baseline (Google Scholar) against an agentic system, giving a concrete comparison point for decision 1, though the huge margin invites scrutiny of benchmark construction (decision 3).
limitations: benchmark (PaSaMaster-Bench) is self-constructed, raising possible construction bias
no ablation isolating self-evolving retrieval's contribution from other components' contribution to the reported gain
relevance_reason: Explicitly measures against a single-query baseline (Google Scholar) and reports a large agentic gain — central to decisions 1 and 2, though its self-reported magnitude is exactly the kind of number decision 4 asks us to interrogate.

key_finding: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on literature search, summarization, and contradiction-detection tasks, and identifies 2.34 ± 1.99 contradictions per paper in biology literature, 70% validated by human experts.
methodology: Human-AI comparison methodology on real-world literature research tasks; introduces the LitQA2 benchmark used to guide PaperQA2's design; humans given unrestricted internet/tool access for a fair comparison.
why_it_matters: The foundational claim the whole 'agentic beats baseline' premise rests on; any replication-failure evidence found later has to be read against this specific benchmark (LitQA2) and comparison protocol.
limitations: benchmark (LitQA2) co-developed with the system it evaluates, raising circularity concerns
biology-heavy evaluation domain limits generality
relevance_reason: The most cited, most direct prior claim that agentic literature-search systems beat human/baseline performance — the paper decision 4 is specifically asking us to stress-test.

key_finding: Across custom (Chronos) and provider-native CLI agent harnesses, grep-based retrieval generally yields higher accuracy than vector retrieval on a 116-question LongMemEval sample, with overall scores depending strongly on harness/tool-calling style even given identical underlying data.
methodology: Two empirical experiments comparing grep vs. vector retrieval across multiple agent harnesses, with inline vs. file-based tool outputs, and with progressively added distractor context.
why_it_matters: Undercuts the assumption that more sophisticated retrieval (embeddings) beats simple lexical search inside agent loops — relevant to decision 1's baseline question and decision 4's search for gains that don't hold up, even though the task is conversational memory rather than literature search.
limitations: evaluated on LongMemEval (conversational memory), not scientific literature retrieval
small sample (116 questions)
relevance_reason: A rare finding where a simpler retrieval baseline (grep) beats a more sophisticated one (vector) inside agent harnesses — exactly the kind of result decision 4 asks the scan to reach for, despite being outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks; GraphRAG-Bench systematically identifies the conditions under which graph structure does and does not provide measurable benefit across fact retrieval, complex reasoning, summarization, and creative generation.
methodology: Introduces GraphRAG-Bench, a benchmark spanning the full GraphRAG pipeline (construction, retrieval, generation) with tasks of increasing difficulty; systematically compares GraphRAG against vanilla RAG.
why_it_matters: Citation-graph traversal in literature-search agents is mechanistically the same operation as knowledge-graph traversal in GraphRAG — both retrieve neighboring nodes via stored graph relations rather than re-querying — so this benchmark's finding that graph traversal often fails to beat vanilla retrieval transfers directly to decision 2's mechanism question and decision 4's replication-failure search.
limitations: evaluated on general RAG tasks, not scientific-literature corpora specifically
graph construction quality may vary by domain, limiting how directly the failure transfers to citation graphs built from papers
relevance_reason: Empirically shows the graph-traversal mechanism named in the brief's decision 2 often fails to beat vanilla retrieval, via the same underlying operation (stored-graph neighbor retrieval) that citation-graph traversal in literature search relies on — the clearest available evidence against the premise that agentic graph mechanisms reliably add gain.

key_finding: DynaKRAG's learned evidence-control policy ranks first in EM/F1 across all nine dataset-backbone pairs (HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue with three LLM backbones) while cutting total-token cost 10.1-34.3% and retrieval calls 15.1-43.4% versus matched baselines.
methodology: Unified state-conditioned policy coordinating iterative retrieval, query reformulation, evidence assessment, and sufficiency checking; evaluated across three multi-hop QA datasets and three LLM backbones.
why_it_matters: Provides an efficiency-focused counterpoint on iterative retrieval and reformulation costs, useful for measuring the cost side of decision 2's gain even though it is validated on QA rather than literature-search corpora.
limitations: multi-hop QA setting, not literature search
gains reported as system-level Pareto dominance rather than attributed to a single isolated operator
relevance_reason: A retrieval/reranking-adjacent method combining iterative retrieval and reformulation with quantified efficiency and accuracy gains, relevant to decision 3's underlying techniques though outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: Search-time contamination inflates deep research agent benchmark performance by up to 4% across six public benchmarks, via benchmark metadata leakage, question-context leakage, or explicit answer leakage during live web search.
methodology: Defines three contamination severity types, develops detection algorithms, and quantifies inflation on modern deep research agents across six public benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Search-time contamination is a generic vulnerability of any web-search-capable deep-research agent, including literature-search agents; the same leakage mechanisms (metadata, question-context, answer leakage) would inflate scores on literature-search benchmarks with web-connected agents, so this finding transfers directly to decision 4's inflation concern and to how decision 3's benchmarks should control access.
limitations: studied on general deep-research-agent benchmarks, not literature-search-specific ones
4% inflation figure may not transfer exactly to closed literature corpora with less web-leakage risk
relevance_reason: Directly quantifies a gain-inflation mechanism (search-time contamination) affecting the class of agentic search systems the brief studies — central evidence for decision 4.

key_finding: Deep Research Bench's 89 multi-step web research tasks show that offline 'RetroSearch' agents (using a frozen scraped web-page set) perform comparably to live-web agents, enabling stable evaluation over time.
methodology: Constructs an 89-task, 8-category benchmark with human-worked answers and a frozen 'RetroSearch' corpus environment; benchmarks major LLMs including thinking models, and evaluates branded 'Deep Research' products.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a benchmark-construction control (frozen corpus) for isolating agent capability from a changing web, informing how a contamination-resistant literature-search benchmark for decision 3 might be built.
limitations: general web research tasks, not scientific literature search specifically
8 task categories may not capture literature-search-specific relevance judgments
relevance_reason: A benchmark-construction case study relevant to decision 3, showing how corpus freezing controls for evaluation drift, though its task domain is general web research rather than scientific literature.

key_finding: The leading MTEB retriever (SFR-Embedding-Mistral, 59.0 nDCG@10 on MTEB) scores only 18.3 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT's reasoning-intensive queries, and incorporating explicit query reasoning improves retrieval by up to 12.2 points.
methodology: Introduces BRIGHT, a 1,384-query text retrieval benchmark spanning economics, psychology, math, and coding, requiring reasoning beyond surface matching; evaluates state-of-the-art retrieval models.
why_it_matters: Establishes, with concrete numbers, how far single-query embedding search's recall ceiling falls once queries require reasoning — analogous evidence for the baseline-ceiling quantity decision 1 needs, though measured outside the literature-search domain.
limitations: queries drawn from economics, psychology, math, and coding, not scientific literature search
does not evaluate agentic (multi-step) retrieval systems, only single-pass retrievers plus a reasoning-augmented variant
relevance_reason: The clearest quantified demonstration that single-query embedding retrieval's ceiling collapses on reasoning-intensive queries — widely cited foundational evidence for decision 1's baseline question, from outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: Agents-K1's pipeline converts 2.46 million scientific papers into agent-native knowledge graphs (Scholar-KG) and demonstrates superior performance in scientific information extraction, knowledge-graph construction, and multi-hop scientific reasoning.
methodology: Combines a five-module multimodal document parser, a 4B GRPO-trained information-extraction backbone, and a tri-source agent interface (web search, multimodal graph retrieval, cross-document traversal); builds and releases a one-million-paper Scholar-KG subset.
why_it_matters: Directly implements citation-graph traversal as a first-class agentic search mechanism over a large real scientific corpus, giving a concrete design to weigh against simpler single-query baselines when assessing decision 2's mechanism question.
limitations: no explicit single-query database search baseline reported for direct recall comparison
no ablation isolating graph-traversal's contribution from parsing/extraction gains
relevance_reason: A large-scale, in-domain system building agent-native scientific knowledge graphs with cross-document (citation-graph) traversal — squarely the system design the brief is scanning for.
